title: Microsoft Winds Down Oracle AI Cloud Rental Deal in Wider Partnership Review
excerpt: Bloomberg reported Microsoft declined to renew the 2023 Oracle contract and has been switching off rented capacity built on an older generation of Nvidia chips; Oracle shares fell nearly 3%.
body:
• Microsoft is winding down an arrangement to rent AI computing capacity from Oracle as part of a larger reassessment of billions of dollars in cloud partnerships, Bloomberg News reported on Friday, citing people familiar with the matter.
  • Microsoft had been turning off rented Oracle capacity in recent months after declining to renew the contract, because the capacity, built on an older generation of Nvidia chips, no longer met its evolving needs, according to the report.
  • Oracle shares were down nearly 3% in afternoon trading on Friday, while Microsoft was little changed, Reuters reported.
  • The deal being wound down dates to 2023, when Oracle announced a multi-year agreement for Microsoft to use Oracle Cloud Infrastructure AI infrastructure to power the AI-assisted version of Bing.

Microsoft is winding down its arrangement to rent artificial intelligence computing capacity from Oracle, Reuters reported on Friday, citing a Bloomberg News report based on people familiar with the matter. The wind-down is part of a larger reassessment of billions of dollars in cloud partnerships, as Microsoft rethinks how it secures computing capacity for its AI investments.

Why the rented capacity lost its value

Microsoft had been turning off rented computing capacity from Oracle in recent months after declining to renew the contract, according to the Bloomberg report. Over time, the rented capacity became less valuable as it no longer met Microsoft's evolving needs, the report added, noting that the Oracle hardware used an older generation of Nvidia chips. Oracle pushed back on any suggestion that demand for that hardware had disappeared.

"Demand for OCI's (Oracle Cloud Infrastructure) AI infrastructure remains strong, including for earlier-generation GPUs."

— Oracle spokesperson, to Reuters

Microsoft did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment, and neither company has announced the wind-down in its own statement. The financial terms of the original arrangement were not disclosed, so the revenue Oracle loses from this specific contract cannot be quantified from the reporting.

The 2023 deal now being unwound

The arrangement dates to November 2023, when Oracle announced a multi-year agreement to support the growth of AI services. Microsoft was to use Oracle Cloud Infrastructure AI infrastructure, along with its own Microsoft Azure AI infrastructure, for inferencing of AI models being optimised to power Microsoft Bing conversational searches daily, using Azure Kubernetes Service to orchestrate OCI Compute at scale through the Oracle Interconnect for Microsoft Azure. That was a moment when demand for AI computing outran any single provider's supply. The reported reason for the exit is the mirror image of that moment: capacity bought for an earlier generation of models and chips no longer fits what Microsoft now needs.

A wider review of rented computing

The Oracle wind-down is not an isolated contract decision. The report adds to signs that Microsoft is rethinking how it secures computing capacity to get more out of its massive AI investments, Reuters said. AI cloud company IREN said on Thursday it had delayed some infrastructure deliveries after Microsoft requested changes to its network design, pushing back IREN's target for bringing more than $4 billion in annualised revenue capacity online from year-end to January, with a possible further delay until late February. Earlier on Thursday, Bloomberg News reported Microsoft was tightening oversight of some data centre projects run by neocloud providers including IREN, Nebius and Nscale amid delays and rising costs, Reuters reported via SRN News.

Market reaction and what to watch

Oracle shares were down nearly 3% in afternoon trading on Friday, while Microsoft was little changed, Reuters reported via Hindu BusinessLine. Both stocks had come under pressure this week after a Democratic midterm election sweep in the United States raised worries about tighter scrutiny that could threaten the AI industry's expansion. What to watch is whether the reassessment produces disclosed contract changes at the other providers named in the reporting, and whether Oracle reports any effect on demand for its cloud infrastructure in its next results. For the large Indian and diaspora workforce across Microsoft, Oracle and their cloud partners, the sourced facts support one conclusion only: a major buyer is consolidating rented AI capacity as hardware generations turn over, and suppliers whose capacity rests on older chips are the first exposed.
